The Atlantic Ocean. The second-largest ocean on Earth, covering approximately twenty percent of its surface and separating the continents of Europe and Africa from North and South America. Formed during the breakup of the supercontinent Pangaea, it has been the primary highway for European exploration, colonization, and trade since the fifteenth century.

The Atlantic is bounded by the coasts of Europe and Africa to the east and the Americas to the west, with the Arctic Ocean to the north and the Southern Ocean to the south. Christopher Columbus's fifteen ninety-two voyage across the Atlantic initiated sustained European contact with the Americas, fundamentally reshaping world history. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain range running the length of the ocean, marks the boundary between the North American and Eurasian plates and the South American and African plates.

The Atlantic's discovery of fossil fuels in continental shelves made it economically critical. The North Sea oil fields remain major global energy sources. The Atlantic was the primary route for the transatlantic slave trade, which forcibly transported over twelve million Africans to the Americas between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Battle of the Atlantic during World War Two was the longest battle of the war, in which German U-boats attacked Allied convoys supplying Britain. The Titanic sank in the Atlantic in nineteen twelve after striking an iceberg, becoming one of the most famous maritime disasters. The Atlantic has an average depth of about three thousand three hundred meters, or eleven thousand feet, and contains major island chains including the Caribbean, Azores, and Canary Islands.

Britain's naval dominance of the Atlantic was central to its imperial power from the seventeenth through early twentieth centuries. The transatlantic slave trade was built on Atlantic shipping routes. The Panama Canal, opened later, revolutionized Atlantic navigation by providing a shortcut to the Pacific without rounding Cape Horn.
